statement: In people who drink, in 19 high-income countries, without known heart or blood-vessel disease at the start (83 cohort studies pooled with individual data; 599,912 people who drank, mean age 57; 40,310 deaths over a median 7.5 years), drinking more than about 100 g of alcohol a week (about 14 g a day, or ten 10-g drinks a week; editors' arithmetic) compared with drinking more than 0 and up to 25 g a week is associated with higher death rates that rise with the amount (Wood et al., 2018; adjusted for age, smoking status and diabetes within sex and study): modelled on US death rates, life expectancy at age 40, compared with people drinking up to 100 g a week, was about 6 months shorter at 100 to 200 g a week, 1 to 2 years shorter at 200 to 350 g and 4 to 5 years shorter above 350 g (men above 196 g, 2.7 years, 2.4 to 3.1); death rates were lowest in the groups below about 100 g a week, in men and women alike, and rose less steeply at older ages. About half of the people who drank reported more than 100 g a week (median 96 g). More drinking went with more strokes, heart failure and deaths from high blood pressure and aortic aneurysm, but slightly fewer heart attacks (hazard ratios per 100 g a week 1.14, 1.09, 1.24, 1.15 and 0.94). Compared with non-drinkers, pooled cohort studies find higher death rates from about 45 g a day (315 g a week; editors' arithmetic): relative risk 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32) at 45 to 64 g and 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47) at 65 g or more after adjustment for study characteristics in 107 cohorts (Zhao et al., 2023), and 1.51 (1.25 to 1.82) at 45 g or more in the 7 cohorts that recruited people at a median age of 55 or younger and compared them with people who had never drunk (Stockwell et al., 2024); at 25 to 44 g a day the pooled estimates were close to no difference (1.05, 0.96 to 1.14; 1.17, 0.98 to 1.40, in the younger cohorts) but higher in women (1.21, 1.08 to 1.36) than in men (1.01, 0.93 to 1.10); and in a 2006 pooled curve the lower death rate was no longer significant above 42 g a day (18 g in women, 38 g in men). The amounts are what people reported, usually once, and intake is mostly under-reported; the 100 g threshold is read from a figure without an interval; people who drank more also smoked more and more often had lower socio-economic status, which the main models allowed for only through smoking status; and people who had cut down because of illness stayed in the lighter groups. These designs cannot show that the extra drinking itself shortened life. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 83 studies of people who drink, death rates were lowest in people drinking up to about 100 grams of alcohol a week (about 14 grams a day) and rose above that. Using the researchers' model, 40-year-olds drinking 100 to 200 grams a week could expect about 6 months less life than those drinking up to 100 grams, 200 to 350 grams about 1 to 2 years less, and more than 350 grams about 4 to 5 years less. About half of the people who drank reported more than 100 grams a week. Compared with people who did not drink, studies found higher death rates from about 45 grams a day, and from about 25 grams a day in women in one analysis. People reported their own drinking, usually once and often less than they drank; people who drank more also smoked more; and those who cut down because of illness were among the lighter drinkers, so the studies cannot show that the extra alcohol itself shortened life.
population: People who drink, in high-income countries: 599,912 current drinkers without known cardiovascular disease in 83 cohorts pooled with individual data (mean age 57, 44% women); and, for comparisons with non-drinkers, adults in the cohort studies pooled in three meta-analyses (34, 87 and 107 cohorts)
exposure: Self-reported alcohol intake: in grams a week in categories from more than 0 to more than 350 g, corrected to long-term average intake (individual data); in grams a day in the meta-analyses (25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 g or more; 45 g or more in the younger cohorts)
comparator: People drinking more than 0 and up to 25 g a week for death rates, and more than 0 and up to 100 g a week for life expectancy (individual data, current drinkers only); in the meta-analyses, non-drinkers as each study defined them, lifetime abstainers as modelled, or each study's lowest-intake category
outcome: Death from any cause; modelled life expectancy at age 40; first stroke, heart failure, heart attack and other cardiovascular events
magnitude: Wood et al. 2018 (83 cohorts; 599,912 current drinkers without known cardiovascular disease; 40,310 deaths; median follow-up 7.5 years; reference more than 0 and up to 25 g a week; adjusted for age, smoking status and diabetes, stratified by sex and study): all-cause mortality lowest below about 100 g a week (category values only in a figure; no interval for the threshold); modelled life expectancy at 40 against more than 0 and up to 100 g a week: about 6 months shorter at more than 100 to 200 g, 1 to 2 years at more than 200 to 350 g, 4 to 5 years above 350 g; men above 112 g a week 1.6 years (1.3 to 1.8), above 196 g 2.7 years (2.4 to 3.1); women above 112 or 98 g about 1.3 years (1.1 to 1.5); per 100 g a week, stroke HR 1.14 (1.10 to 1.17), heart failure 1.09 (1.03 to 1.15), fatal hypertensive disease 1.24 (1.15 to 1.33), fatal aortic aneurysm 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), coronary disease other than heart attack 1.06 (1.00 to 1.11), heart attack 0.94 (0.91 to 0.97); about 50% of current drinkers above 100 g a week (median 96 g). Against non-drinkers (study level): Zhao et al. 2023, fully adjusted, 25 to 44 g a day 1.05 (0.96 to 1.14), 45 to 64 g 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32), 65 g or more 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47); men 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10), 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), 1.34 (1.23 to 1.47); women 1.21 (1.08 to 1.36), 1.34 (1.11 to 1.63), 1.61 (1.44 to 1.80); Stockwell et al. 2016, limited adjustment 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00), 1.12 (1.07 to 1.17), 1.29 (1.22 to 1.36), all study-level covariates 1.07 (0.97 to 1.18), 1.24 (1.12 to 1.37), 1.44 (1.30 to 1.60); Stockwell et al. 2024, cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger against lifetime abstainers, 25 to under 45 g 1.17 (0.98 to 1.40), 45 g or more 1.51 (1.25 to 1.82), former drinkers 1.32 (1.13 to 1.54); Di Castelnuovo et al. 2006, lower mortality no longer significant above 42 g a day (men 38 g, women 18 g), and the fitted curves cross a relative risk of 1 at about 44 g a day (men 41 g, women 25 g; editors' calculation from the printed parameters). Unit conversions (editors' arithmetic): 100 g a week is about 14 g a day; 45 g a day is 315 g a week; 25 g a day is 175 g a week.

Over 5.4 million person-years (median follow-up 7.5 years) there were 40,310 deaths.

evidence.extracted: About 50% of current drinkers reported more than 100 g of alcohol a week (median 96 g a week); intake was weakly positively correlated with male sex, smoking and lower socio-economic status. All-cause mortality rose with intake in a positive, curvilinear association, lowest for categories below about 100 g a week, relative to current drinkers of more than 0 and up to 25 g a week; similar in men and women and weaker at older ages. Models were adjusted for age, smoking status and history of diabetes and stratified by sex and study. The category results appear only in a figure and an appendix, and the threshold is stated without an interval.

evidence.extracted: Higher doses of alcohol were associated with increased mortality. The lower mortality was no longer significant above 42 g a day for all 56 curves, above 38 g in men (32 adjusted curves) and above 18 g in women (16 adjusted curves); the curves of men and women differed, protection being apparent up to 3 drinks a day in men and 2 in women. Fitted parameters: all curves b1 = −0.1592 and b2 = 0.0421; women −0.1719 and 0.0533; men −0.1445 and 0.0388. The authors add that under-reporting of intake would bias relative risks towards the null and may have distorted the apparent threshold for harm. Editors' calculation from these parameters (log RR = b1√x + b2√x·log x, fixed-effect point estimates, no intervals): the fitted curves cross a relative risk of 1 at about 44 g a day for all curves, 41 g for men and 25 g for women.

risk_of_bias.note: Wood et al. (ROBINS-E high on card sc_wood_2018): the main models adjust only for age, smoking status (current or not) and diabetes within sex and study; people who cut down because of illness stay in the lighter groups (residual reverse causation, acknowledged by the authors); intake was self-reported once and corrected for regression dilution from about 12% of participants. The meta-analyses compared with non-drinkers that include former drinkers in most cohorts and are critically low on AMSTAR 2.

inconsistency.note: Every analysis finds higher death rates at heavier intake; where the rise begins differs with the comparison (the lightest drinkers or non-drinkers) and, against non-drinkers, with sex (25 to 44 g a day: women 1.21, men 1.01), which explains rather than contradicts.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: people who drink, mostly middle-aged and older, in high-income countries; the life-expectancy differences are modelled on US death rates for 2007 to 2010, which the claim says.

imprecision.note: Large numbers (40,310 deaths in the individual data); the threshold itself has no interval because it is read from plotted category results, which the claim states as 'about'.

publication_bias.note: Egger tests found none in the 2016 and 2023 meta-analyses; not assessable for the pooled individual data.

large_effect.note: No category ratio above 2 is printed in the texts read.

dose_response.note: Death rates and modelled life-expectancy losses rise step by step with intake above about 100 g a week (about 6 months, 1 to 2 years, 4 to 5 years), and across the meta-analyses' categories (for example 1.05, 1.19 and 1.35 at 25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 g a day or more), in individual data from 83 cohorts and in study-level data from 107.

plausible_confounding.note: Reverse causation from people who cut down because of illness would make the lighter groups look worse and hide part of the rise, while smoking and lower socio-economic status, which rise with intake, could add to it; they pull in opposite directions; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low, is rated down once for risk of bias and up once for a dose-response gradient: low. The upgrade is made although the evidence was rated down, because the gradient appears within people who drink (no abstainer comparison is needed for it), in individual data from 83 cohorts, and again in study-level data compared with non-drinkers; a strict reading that withholds the upgrade, because smoking and lower socio-economic status also rise with intake and the main models allow only for smoking status, gives very low. Worded as an association: these designs cannot show that the extra drinking caused the deaths. Status replicated: Wood et al. (a consortium analysis of 83 cohorts), the Stockwell–Zhao group's analyses (counted once) and Di Castelnuovo et al. are different teams whose estimates all rise at heavier intake, though they may share some cohorts; the threshold of about 100 g a week itself rests on one pooled analysis.
